opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The motivation came from a very practical pain point. When we started TVM, deep learning was exploding in two directions at once: there were more and more models, with new operators and new combinations of operators showing up all the time, and there was a growing zoo of hardware: different generations of GPUs, mobile CPUs, embedded devices, and all these new accelerators people were starting to build.

The way the ecosystem handled that was mostly by hand. Vendors and framework developers would write highly optimized kernel libraries, things like cuDNN or MKL, and each of those kernels took real expert effort to tune for a specific operator, shape, and piece of hardware. That works if you have a small number of operators and one or two dominant platforms. But once you multiply the number of operators by the number of shapes by the number of hardware targets, the engineering cost becomes enormous. Some combinations just never got optimized, and that slows down both new models and new hardware.

So the question we asked was: can we treat kernel optimization as a machine learning and search problem itself, instead of something only a handful of experts can do by hand? The first step was separating *what* you compute from *how* you compute it, the schedule, an idea we borrowed and extended from Halide. Once you have that separation, there's a large space of possible implementations for the same computation. The next step was to search that space automatically, using a learned cost model to predict which candidates would be fast so we didn't have to measure everything on real hardware. That became AutoTVM, and later Ansor and MetaSchedule pushed it further by needing fewer hand-written templates.

The deeper reason I cared about it is that I think of machine learning systems as a full-stack problem. If the bottom layer, the kernels, is fixed and hand-written, you're limited in what you can do with fusion, new data types, or new hardware. Automatic kernel generation makes the whole stack more open: a new accelerator team or a researcher with a weird new operator can get reasonable performance without waiting for someone to hand-tune it. In a sense, it's about using ML to make ML systems more accessible, and that's always been something I find really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says the number of operators, shapes, and hardware targets multiplies into enormous engineering costs, leaving some combinations unoptimized—clearly explaining why handwritten kernels cannot keep pace.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that it came out of pain. Around the time we were building XGBoost and then MXNet, every time a new operator showed up, or a new piece of hardware, somebody had to sit down and hand-write a kernel for it. And not just one kernel. You'd write it for NVIDIA GPUs, then someone would ask about ARM, then a mobile GPU, then an FPGA, and each of those is a different person with a different skill set and weeks of tuning. The number of operators times the number of hardware backends was growing much faster than the number of people who could do that kind of work.

So when we started TVM, the thing I kept coming back to was that most of what those engineers were doing wasn't creative in the mathematical sense. The math of a convolution or a matmul doesn't change. What changes is loop ordering, tiling, how you map to threads, when you vectorize, how you use shared memory. Those are all decisions in a fairly well-defined space. And if it's a space, you can describe it, and if you can describe it, a machine can search it.

That was the bet. Separate the "what" from the "how." Let the user write the computation once, and let the compiler, with some help from learned cost models, explore the schedule space and find something competitive with a hand-tuned library. If that worked, it would mean a new accelerator could get decent performance on day one instead of after a year of library engineering. And it would mean a new operator that a researcher invented on Tuesday could run fast on Wednesday instead of waiting for a vendor to prioritize it.

I also think there was a deeper point about where the leverage is. Hardware is diversifying, models are diversifying, and the only thing that scales across both of those axes is automation. Hand-written kernels are a dead end as a strategy, even though individually they're excellent. So it felt less like one optimization among many and more like the central problem TVM had to get right for the rest of the system to matter.

r001.rationale: The response says each operator and hardware backend required its own hand-written, tuned kernel, and that the combinations were growing faster than the number of people able to build them.

astra-6.text:
When we were building TVM, one thing we realized was that compiling a model into calls to existing libraries only gets you so far. Those libraries depend on experts writing and tuning kernels for each operator and each piece of hardware. When you have a new operator, or want to fuse several operators together, or target a new device, you need to do that work again.

So the question was: can we automate more of that process? We wanted developers to describe what they wanted to compute, and let the system explore how to execute it efficiently—things like how to tile the computation, organize memory access, and parallelize the work.

That was important because we wanted TVM to support a broad range of models and hardware. Automatic kernel generation offered a way to get good performance without having to manually build an optimized library for every combination.

r001.rationale: The response says experts must retune kernels for new operators, fused operators, and devices, and that TVM aimed to avoid manually building a library for every combination. It does not clearly state that the variant space is too large for handwritten implementation to keep pace.

sol-6.1.text:
When we started thinking about TVM, one of the key challenges was the diversity of hardware. You have CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators, and each of them needs very different optimizations to run a machine learning workload efficiently. Traditionally, that performance comes from experts manually writing and tuning kernels for each platform.

But there are also many different models, with different operators and tensor shapes. If you need to hand-optimize every combination of workload and hardware, it becomes very difficult to keep up. And if a compiler still depends on someone supplying all those optimized kernels, that limits how easily it can support new hardware or new models.

So we saw automatic kernel generation as a way to address that bottleneck. Can we describe the computation, express the possible ways to optimize it, and let the system search for an efficient implementation on the target hardware? That was important for making TVM both portable and performant, while reducing the amount of manual engineering needed.

r001.rationale: The response says that many models, operators, tensor shapes, and hardware combinations make hand-optimizing every case difficult to keep up with, clearly conveying that handwritten kernel variants cannot scale to the size of the space.
